questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule letting the people vote the convention's draft
questions.learningObjective: Explain the rule that submitted a convention's draft to the voters
questions.stem: Nitrate crept up overnight, and I wrote out in the logbook the rule that sent a convention's draft to the voters, and what the rule was meant to secure.

answer.exemplar: A convention assembled to draft a new constitution was made of delegates, and delegates alone might have produced a text that the people had never seen. The rule that sent the draft to the electorate was meant to close that gap. The finished draft was published, laid before the voters, and accepted or rejected by them, so that the government of the state rested on a text the body of the people had judged acceptable rather than on a text merely drafted by chosen delegates. The rule also fixed the question: the vote was on the whole draft, so the people accepted or rejected a constitution rather than a series of separate provisions.

questions.explanation: Sending the draft to the voters placed the constitution's authority beyond the convention that wrote it, and the vote was on the whole draft. It was a check on the delegates, not a step in the drafting.
questions.hint: The people voted on the finished draft.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A sewer and the disease it was meant to stop
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sewer was argued to be a measure against sickness
questions.stem: Fry hid in the rock crevice, and I explained in the logbook why a sewer was argued to be a measure against sickness, and what it could not do by itself.

answer.exemplar: The argument ran that the illnesses which killed the townspeople travelled in the water and in the waste, and that a city's own filth, discharged where it was drunk, was returning to the people it killed. A sewer that carried the waste away from the town, and a clean water supply to replace it, would therefore break the circle, and the deaths from cholera and typhoid would fall. The limit of the argument was equally clear to its makers. A sewer was only half of the work: a clean supply of water had to come with it, because a city that flushed its streets and then drank from the same water upstream had changed nothing except the plumbing. Where the supply remained fouled, the sewer alone could be seen to change nothing at all.

questions.explanation: The sewer broke the circle that returned the town's waste to its water supply, but it was half a remedy, and without clean water it changed nothing. The two had to come together.
questions.hint: A sewer alone was only half the work.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The clock and the factory
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the factory clock did and the difficulty it created
questions.stem: The calcium reactor stalled, and I explained in the logbook what the clock did in the factory, and the difficulty it created for the employer.

answer.exemplar: Before the clock, a day's work was measured by the task and by the man who judged whether it was done. The factory clock replaced the foreman's estimate with a number, and that was its value: the hours of every worker became comparable, and pay could be settled by the record rather than by dispute. The difficulty came from the same source. Once time was the measure, the employer had an interest in how much was done within the hour, and the pace of work became a question of management rather than of custom. The clock that removed one kind of uncertainty introduced another, and the discipline of the workshop grew out of the attempt to settle the second one.

questions.explanation: The clock turned the day's work into a comparable number, so pay could be settled from the record instead of dispute. Its very success raised the harder question of how much was done within the hour.
questions.hint: Time became the measure of the work.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mortgage holder using his own inspection report
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a lender wanted its own inspection and what trouble followed
questions.stem: Lighting cycle ran long in the tank, and I explained in the logbook why a lending institution wanted its own inspection of a property, and what trouble the arrangement carried.

answer.exemplar: The institution wanted its own inspection because the value of the property was the basis of the whole transaction, and the inspection was quicker and cheaper than a negotiation with the borrower over a figure. It also told the borrower what the loan would be, which spared both parties a dispute at the last moment. The trouble sat in the same arrangement. The inspector was paid by the institution and answered to it, and the pressure to write a generous figure came from the borrower's side of the table, where a larger loan was wanted and a business was waiting to borrow. An official valued by the lender was efficient and consistent, and he was also not an independent witness to the value he was reporting.

questions.stem: Hydrometer reading drifted warm in the evening, and I explained in the logbook how the chain store took the independent retailer out of business, and what it cost the small shop.

answer.exemplar: The independent retailer had bought his stock as he thought best and had set his own prices, and he had no particular reason to lose either habit. The chain store bought in quantities that no single shop could reach, took the discounts the manufacturers gave for volume, and sold the goods below what the small shop could afford to sell them for. The customer moved, and the small shop was left buying at the wholesaler's prices while selling at the chain's. questions.explanation: The chain used bulk buying and low prices to take the custom, and the same arrangements that made the price possible also took the choice of stock from the small shop. Price and supply did the work together.
questions.hint: Bulk buying, lower prices, stock chosen elsewhere.

questions.stem: A brittle star moved the rubble under the sand, and I explained in the logbook how a law about truthful labelling grew out of published analysis, and the change it made.

answer.exemplar: The earlier law had been built on the promise of the manufacturer, on the label that the maker put on his own goods, and a promise of that kind settled nothing between a dishonest seller and a careful buyer. The change came when a government laboratory began to buy ordinary products from the shops, examine them, and publish what was found, so that the fact of the adulteration was no longer a matter of private suspicion but of public record. options.misconception: Makes the sewer a land-reclamation work

questions.explanation: The sewer was for carrying waste away, and the case for it was made pressing by outbreaks that returned in a city already known to be filthy. It was not a water supply or a graveyard measure.
questions.hint: Waste removed, and outbreaks that kept coming back.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The clock and the factory
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a works rule on the clock as the measure of time

stimulus.body: I copied this from the works rule book: no man shall leave his place before the hour, nor return to it after the hour, without leave from the foreman, and the time of the clock at the gate shall be the time of all.

questions.stem: A shrimp was found molting in the rock pool, and I set the rule into the logbook and asked what the rule shows about the shift in authority over the workers' time.

options.text: That the clock, and not the foreman's judgement, became the measure of the workers' time
That the workers' own sense of the day's work was replaced by a record of hours kept
options.misconception: Substitutes hours kept for the worker's own account

options.text: That the foreman gained the right to grant leave whenever he thought the work allowed
options.misconception: Turns the leave clause into a discretionary power

options.text: That the rules shortened the working day of the men employed in the trade
options.misconception: Claims the rules cut the hours

questions.explanation: The rule made the gate clock the measure of the workers' time and turned the day's work into a matter of hours kept, so the foreman's judgement no longer governed it. It granted no general leave.
questions.hint: The gate clock measures the time.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The chain that ended the independent retailer
questions.learningObjective: Summarise what the chain store did to the independent retailer
questions.stem: Timer failed to switch the light on the reef tank, and I wrote the summary of what the chain store did to the independent retailer, and the moral the summary carries.

options.text: The retailer was not beaten by argument but by buying, so the small shop had to change its buying or go
The retailer was beaten by the law, which forbade small shops to sell below price
options.misconception: Makes the law the agent of the chain

options.text: The retailer was beaten by the quality of the chain's goods, which were plainly better
options.misconception: Explains the outcome by quality rather than price

options.text: The retailer was beaten by the transport, which moved goods to the chain's store more cheaply
options.misconception: Makes transport the deciding advantage

questions.explanation: The chain prevailed through buying, not through argument, law, quality, or transport, and the small shop had to join the buying arrangements or withdraw. The moral concerns the power of the buying office.
questions.hint: Buying, not arguing, decided it.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule letting the people vote the convention's draft
questions.learningObjective: State who decided the draft under the rule of submission
questions.stem: The new fish refused food for three days, and I wrote in the logbook who decided the constitution's draft under the rule of submission, and who did not.

options.text: The people decided it by their vote, and the convention that drafted it had no final power
The convention decided it by its own vote, and the people only ratified what it had done
options.misconception: Turns ratification into a rubber stamp of the convention

options.text: The legislature decided it, after the people had expressed their opinion upon the draft
options.misconception: Gives the legislature the deciding vote

options.text: The governor decided it, in the exercise of the power to refer a question to the people
options.misconception: Makes the governor the deciding authority

questions.explanation: The people's vote decided the draft, and the drafting convention retained no final power over it. The legislature and the governor had no deciding part in the constitution itself.
questions.hint: The vote of the people, and nothing after it.

questions.topic: From a truthful label to a published analysis
questions.learningObjective: State what the law of truthful labels required of the maker
questions.stem: Sump was louder than usual, and I wrote in the logbook what the law requiring truthful labels required of the maker, and what it did not require.

options.text: That the label declare what the product contained, and any substance added to it
That the maker disclose the price at which the product had been bought
options.misconception: Invents a disclosure of cost

options.text: That the maker publish the name of every man employed in the making of the goods
options.misconception: Invents a disclosure of employees

options.text: That the maker sell the product only to buyers holding a printed certificate of analysis

options.text: They built sewers to carry the waste away from the inhabited streets
They brought in a supply of water that had not been fouled by the town
They kept records of the deaths from the diseases the works were meant to prevent
They closed every well in the district at the first report of sickness

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mortgage holder using his own inspection report
questions.learningObjective: Summarise what a lender's own inspection did for the loan
questions.stem: Grab samples were nearly empty of life, and I wrote the summary of what a lending institution's own inspection of a property did for the loan, and what it left unsettled.

options.text: It fixed the figure the loan would rest on, and left unsettled whether that figure was the right one
It fixed the figure and made it unanswerable, so no dispute about value was possible
options.misconception: Claims the inspection made the valuation unchallengeable

options.text: It left the figure entirely open, and the amount was settled by negotiation alone
options.misconception: Turns the inspection into no valuation at all

options.text: It fixed the figure for the lender only, and the borrower was never told what it was
options.misconception: Says the borrower was kept in the dark

questions.explanation: The inspection fixed the figure on which the loan rested, and the value of that figure remained arguable, since the report was the institution's own judgment. The borrower was told the figure and could dispute it.
questions.hint: A figure fixed, and a figure still arguable.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why coal and steam broke the siting constraint
questions.learningObjective: State what a factorymaster's engine purchase turned on
questions.stem: Weedy patch cleared in a week after the light change, and I wrote in the logbook what a factorymaster's decision to buy an engine turned on, and what it freed him from.

options.text: On freedom from the site, since the works could stand where the coal and the labour were
On freedom from the weather, since the engine did not depend upon a fall of water
options.misconception: Turns the freedom from site into freedom from weather

options.text: On freedom from the law, since an engine was not subject to the mill rights of the stream
options.misconception: Invents a legal freedom the engine did not give

options.text: On freedom from the wage bill, since the engine needed no hands at all
options.misconception: Claims the engine removed the need for workers

questions.explanation: The decision turned on freedom from the site, since the works could then stand where the coal and the labour were. The engine did not free the master from weather, law, or the wage bill.
questions.hint: Free from the site, to follow coal and hands.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The clock and the factory
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the factory clock did to the worker's day
questions.stem: Glass was cold to the touch, and I explained in the logbook what the factory clock did to the worker's day, and the trouble the employer had with it.

answer.exemplar: The clock turned the working day from a stretch of daylight into a quantity that could be counted, and the worker felt the change before the employer did. A day that had been begun and ended with the light, and had been made longer or shorter by the season and the weather, became eight hours or ten, the same on a Monday as in June, and the whole life of the workshop was arranged around that number. For the employer the trouble was that the number settled only the length of the day and not the work within it. Time was now measurable and therefore valuable, which meant that every minute saved by a worker became visible, and a system of pay that rewarded speed became both a temptation and a grievance. The clock that brought order to the day also made the question of the pace of the work impossible to avoid.

questions.explanation: The clock turned the day into a fixed number regardless of light and season, which the worker felt, and it settled the length of the day but not the work within it, making the pace unavoidable.
questions.hint: The day counted, the pace undecided.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: From a truthful label to a published analysis
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the method of the investigation as a guarantee of its fairness

stimulus.body: I copied this from the account of the analysis: the samples were bought in the ordinary way at retail prices in several cities, and the results of each examination were published in a bulletin which was distributed widely and quoted in the newspapers.

questions.stem: Filter socks were pink with debris, and I read the account into the logbook and asked what the method of the investigation was meant to ensure.

options.text: That the samples were ordinary goods bought openly, so the findings would match what buyers got
That the examiners had bought the goods from the manufacturer at a discount
options.misconception: Turns the retail purchase into a trade purchase

options.text: That the goods were taken by warrant from the makers' own warehouses
options.misconception: Invents a seizure of samples

options.text: That the makers were invited to send a sample of their own choosing for the test
options.misconception: Turns the investigation into a submission of samples

questions.explanation: Buying openly at retail in several cities was meant to make the findings match what an ordinary buyer received, and publication carried them to the public. Makers were not asked for samples.
questions.hint: Ordinary goods, bought openly, and published.
